transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-07
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 50 minutes
Attendees: Ava Reynolds (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (VectorHealth Head of ML), Ethan Brooks (Infra), Sofia Gomez (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): quick benchmark review comparing Redwood hosted/dedicated to baseline provider, discussed tuning (batching, quantization), agreed on next soak test and deliverables.

00:00 - Ava Reynolds: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check-in saving calendar, uh, the plan today is to run through the benchmark numbers we sent, highlight differences vs the baseline provider, and then go over next steps for the dedicated soak.
00:12 - Maya Patel: Thanks, Ava. We got the spreadsheet, skimmed it. Just to set context, our main SLO is p95 latency under 150ms for the 512-token average workload and sustained throughput to serve ~600 reqs/min during peak. Cost per token also matters because of volume.
00:30 - Liam Chen: Yep that’s what we focused on. Quick caveat, these are synthetic runs using the prompt templates you sent last week; numbers change a bit with your production distribution, but this is a comparable baseline run against BaselineAI.
01:05 - Ethan Brooks: Quick Q — were the BaselineAI runs run in their managed endpoint or a dedicated instance? We need apples to apples.
01:12 - Liam Chen: Good call. BaselineAI numbers are from their managed endpoint with autoscale; our baseline runs for Redwood were both hosted shared and a dedicated config we spun up to approximate their dedicated offering. We left them with default batching so we could compare out of the box performance.
01:45 - Ava Reynolds: Ok jumping into numbers — for the 512-token avg scenario: BaselineAI p95 was ~180ms, throughput about 220 tokens/sec per instance; Redwood hosted p95 was ~120ms, throughput ~350 tokens/sec. Dedicated with batching and warm KV cache pushed p95 down to ~85-95ms and throughput up to ~1,000 tokens/sec in our 4-GPU pool profiling.
02:15 - Sofia Gomez: Sorry can you repeat the dedicated throughput number? That sounds much higher than we expected.
02:18 - Liam Chen: Sure — on the dedicated 4xA100-like config with continuous batching and optimized kernels we measured sustained aggregate throughput ~1k tokens/sec. Per-GPU it scales but the cluster routing optimized for parallelism. There’s variance with sequence length and batching window.
02:50 - Maya Patel: Interesting. How about cold-starts and tail latency? Our traffic spikes matter a lot.
03:05 - Liam Chen: We did cold vs warm runs. Cold first-token penalty is higher — cold p95 can be ~250-300ms on host start for large models. But with caching (prefix/KV) and warm workers, cold incidents are rare; warm p95 drops to the numbers I quoted. We also instrumented KV cache hits, warm runs with hot cache lowered p95 to ~70-80ms in some sequences.
03:40 - Ethan Brooks: Those cold numbers are worrying if we get scaling events. Do you have autoscaling delta times?
03:52 - Liam Chen: Autoscale to spin up a new worker can be ~60-120s depending on infra; we recommend configured burst capacity and pre-warmed headrooms for SLOs. Dedicated lets us keep steady capacity and scale faster within the reserved pool.
04:18 - Maya Patel: What about model variants and quantization — do we lose much quality going to 4-bit?
04:30 - Liam Chen: Good news: for your LLM family (we used an open-vic-ish model variant) 8-bit gives negligible quality loss, 4-bit trimmed some edge-case logits causing slight divergence on very long-context prompts. We did automated evals; ROUGE/BLEU-ish proxies were within 1.5% for 4-bit, and subjective eval flagged some hallucination bumps in very long generations. We can tie specific prompt sets for you to verify.
05:10 - Maya Patel: So tradeoff is cost and throughput vs slight quality drop. VectorHealth is risk-averse on hallucinations, so we probably prefer 8-bit for production unless 4-bit is validated on our prompts.
05:30 - Ava Reynolds: Makes sense. We'll run a 4-bit check limited to low-risk paths and include a quality gating step.
05:40 - Sofia Gomez: Can you summarize cost delta? We need to see hosted vs dedicated numbers.
05:48 - Ava Reynolds: Sure — rough hosted per-token cost in our runs was about $0.00042/token; BaselineAI quoted around $0.00065/token for similar throughput. Dedicated amortized compute costs for the pilot look to bring unit costs down by about 30-45% depending on utilization — we’ll put precise numbers in the spreadsheet. Those are ballpark and depend on quantization and batching.
06:20 - Maya Patel: Where can we see the raw logs and the tests? We want to run them through our latency profiler.
06:27 - Ava Reynolds: Spreadsheet link and raw logs are at: https://redwood.sheets/benchmark-run-2026-03-06 (note: internal link) and raw logs S3: s3://redwood-poc/vectorhealth/2026-03-06 — we'll send IAM presigned links.
06:45 - Ethan Brooks: On security and VPC — if we go dedicated, what's the network architecture? Do you support customer-managed VPC peering or private link?
06:55 - Liam Chen: Yes, we support VPC peering and private link. For Private deployment we can do customer-managed networking and HSM/KMS integrations. We'll send the architecture diagram and SOC2 docs.
07:20 - Maya Patel: Great. Two technical items: 1) can you rerun with our 90th percentile prompt length distribution (we sent last week) and 2) please include cold-start histograms so we can see tail behavior?
07:34 - Liam Chen: Yep that's in the action items — we'll add the 90th distribution and run cold/warm histograms and quantized profiles.
07:45 - Ava Reynolds: Quick note on batching policy — we tested small batching windows (20-30ms) which improves throughput but adds a bit to median latency; you can tune per-route. For your real-time UI, we recommend tighter windows on critical routes and relaxed batching on background batch jobs.
08:10 - Sofia Gomez: Any concerns about model fallbacks if capacity is constrained? For example should we route to a slightly smaller model?
08:18 - Liam Chen: Absolutely — routing policies can fallback to a cheaper, slightly smaller variant. We implement automated fallback with quality thresholds and we can run a brief A/B to see impact. That’s a good lever to keep SLOs during spikes while controlling cost.
08:40 - Maya Patel: On observability, do you provide token-level traces and per-request cost attributions?
08:46 - Ava Reynolds: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost/latency breakdown and trace links. We'll include sample screenshots in the follow-up email.
09:00 - Ethan Brooks: For the dedicated soak test, what's the time we should expect for stable numbers? 2 hours? 4 hours?
09:08 - Liam Chen: Based on variance we recommend a 4-hour soak at production distribution, plus a shorter 30-minute warm-up. That helps expose tail events.
09:20 - Ava Reynolds: Ok to recap actions: Redwood shares updated spreadsheet + raw logs presigned links; SE reruns quantized and 90th distribution cold/warm tests; VectorHealth shares request logs and confirms soak timing; Redwood sends security docs + cost model; follow-up on 2026-03-17 to review soak.
09:40 - Maya Patel: That works. One more ask — can you include noise-injection tests for noisy inputs (we see many OCR artifacts) to test hallucination rates?
09:48 - Liam Chen: Yes we can add a noise-injection suite and include hallucination metrics.
10:00 - Ava Reynolds: Great, thanks everyone. We'll email the notes and links. Meeting adjourned.

Transcript notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings (e.g., open-vic-ish), filler words, and speaker label jitter as this is automated Fireflies export.
